questions.question: How does the book distinguish "data ingestion" from "data integration"?
options: Data ingestion is movement of data from point A to B; data integration combines data from multiple disparate sources into a new dataset
Ingestion only applies to streaming data, while integration only applies to batch data
Ingestion and integration are simply two names for the identical process
Integration means deleting duplicate records; ingestion means writing new ones
questions.explanation: The book states: "Whereas data ingestion is data movement from point A to B, data integration combines data from disparate sources into a new dataset," giving a CRM+ads+web-analytics example.

questions.question: The book says "all data is unbounded until it's bounded." What does this mean, and what role do streaming ingestion systems play?
options: Data in reality flows continuously (unbounded); batches are an artificial boundary imposed for convenience — streaming systems exist to preserve that continuous nature through the pipeline
It means all data eventually disappears if not batched within 24 hours
It means streaming systems convert unbounded data into a single static file
It means bounded data can never be converted back into a stream
questions.explanation: The book explains: "Business processes have long imposed artificial bounds on data by cutting discrete batches... streaming ingestion systems are simply a tool for preserving the unbounded nature of data."

questions.question: Why does the book put "real-time" in quotation marks and prefer the term "near real-time"?
options: No ingestion system is truly instantaneous — every database, queue, or pipeline has inherent latency delivering data to a target system
Because "real-time" systems are always slower than equivalent batch systems
Because the term "real-time" is a trademarked vendor term the authors avoid
Because near real-time applies only to IoT sensor data, never other data types
questions.explanation: The book states: "no ingestion system is genuinely real-time. Any database, queue or pipeline has inherent latency in delivering data to a target system. It is more accurate to speak of near real-time."

questions.question: A legacy ETL system runs dozens of tightly coupled steps, where any single failure forces the entire 24+ hour pipeline to restart from scratch. What pattern is this, and what alternative does the book recommend?
options: Synchronous ingestion — tightly coupled, dependent stages; asynchronous ingestion (processing events individually as they arrive) avoids this all-or-nothing fragility
This describes asynchronous ingestion, with synchronous ingestion being the recommended fix
This describes push ingestion, with pull ingestion being the recommended fix
This is an unavoidable property of all batch systems, with no alternative available
questions.explanation: The book's own case study describes exactly this synchronous failure mode, then contrasts it with asynchronous ingestion where "each stage of the asynchronous pipeline can process data items as they become available in parallel."

questions.question: What are the two general strategies for extracting data from a source system, and how do they differ?
options: Full snapshot (grab the entire current state each time) versus differential/incremental (pull only what changed since the last read) — snapshots are simpler but use more resources
"Hot" versus "cold" extraction, referring to the physical temperature of the source server
"Push" versus "poll," which describe direction rather than extraction scope
"Synchronous" versus "streaming," which are unrelated ingestion concepts
questions.explanation: The book states: "With full snapshots, engineers grab the entire current state... With the differential update pattern, engineers can pull only the updates and changes since the last read."

questions.question: What advantage does file-based export/ingestion offer over a direct database connection, per the book?
options: It avoids exposing backend systems directly — source-system engineers keep full control over what's exported and how it's preprocessed, since export logic runs on the source side
File-based ingestion is always faster than every direct connection method
File-based ingestion eliminates the need for any schema information at all
File-based ingestion is the only method that can support streaming data
questions.explanation: The book notes: "With file-based ingestion, export processes are run on the data-source side, giving source system engineers complete control over what data gets exported and how the data is preprocessed."

questions.question: A team performs many single-row INSERT/UPDATE operations against a columnar analytics database and sees performance degrade badly. What's happening, and what's the better approach?
options: Small-batch operations force many small, suboptimal files and force column-file scans on update — batching fewer, larger operations (or using a tool built for high insert rates) performs much better
Columnar databases cannot perform any inserts or updates under any circumstances
The problem described is purely a network bandwidth issue, unrelated to batch size
A row-based database would perform even worse in this exact same scenario
questions.explanation: The book warns single-row inserts force "many small, suboptimal files," and updates are worse still since they "cause the database to scan each existing column file," recommending purpose-built tools like Druid/Pinot instead.

questions.question: In stream ingestion, what's the difference between "at-least-once" delivery and message ordering issues, and why do both need handling?
options: At-least-once delivery means a message might be processed more than once; ordering issues mean messages may arrive out of sequence — both are inherent distributed-systems risks needing idempotent or order-aware handling
At-least-once delivery automatically guarantees strict message ordering, so no extra handling is needed
Ordering problems only occur in batch pipelines, never in streaming ones
These are two names describing the exact same underlying issue
questions.explanation: The book states streaming platforms "can cause some complications... messages may be delivered out of order and more than once (at-least-once delivery)" — two distinct risks requiring separate handling strategies.

questions.question: What is "replay" in a streaming ingestion platform, and which platform named in the book does NOT support it well?
options: Replay lets you rewind and reread a range of historical events — Kafka, Kinesis, and Pub/Sub support it, but RabbitMQ typically deletes messages once all subscribers have consumed them
Replay means automatically retrying a failed message exactly once
Every platform mentioned in the book supports replay identically
Replay only exists in batch systems, never any streaming platform
questions.explanation: The book states: "RabbitMQ typically deletes messages after all subscribers consume them. Kafka, Kinesis, and Pub/Sub all support event retention and replay."

questions.question: What is a dead-letter queue, and when does an event typically end up there?
options: A separate location for events that couldn't be successfully ingested (e.g. sent to a nonexistent topic, oversized, or expired past TTL), so they don't block other messages and can be diagnosed later
A queue that archives every successfully processed message
A queue reserved exclusively for the highest-priority events
A synonym for a schema registry that tracks schema version history
questions.explanation: The book explains: "Events that cannot be ingested need to be rerouted and stored in a separate location called a dead-letter queue," citing nonexistent topics, oversized messages, or expired TTL as causes.

questions.question: Why does the book say JDBC/ODBC connections are "beginning to show their age" for some modern data engineering use cases?
options: They struggle with nested data (which must be reencoded as strings) and send data row by row, forcing columnar data to be reserialized as rows
JDBC and ODBC no longer work with any relational databases at all
JDBC/ODBC connections cannot be used from Python under any circumstances
JDBC and ODBC require a dedicated physical hardware appliance to function
questions.explanation: The book states: "These connection standards struggle with nested data... native nested data must be reencoded as string data... and columns from columnar databases must be reserialized as rows."

questions.question: What's the key limitation of batch-oriented CDC that continuous, log-based CDC avoids?
options: Batch CDC only captures the latest state since the last check, missing intermediate changes (e.g. several withdrawals in 24 hours show only the final balance); continuous CDC captures every individual change as an event
Batch CDC cannot be used with relational databases at all
Continuous CDC cannot support real-time analytics, only batch reporting
Batch CDC only works with NoSQL databases, never relational ones
questions.explanation: The book's own bank-account example shows this directly: querying changes over 24 hours "will return only the last account balance recorded... other records over the period won't appear," unlike continuous CDC.

questions.question: How does the book distinguish synchronous (tightly coupled) database replication from asynchronous CDC-based replication?
options: Synchronous replication keeps a replica fully in sync with zero data loss on failover but typically requires the same database type on both sides; asynchronous CDC replication is looser, may lag slightly, but can target varied destinations
Synchronous replication is always cheaper and universally preferred over asynchronous replication
Asynchronous replication is impossible between two databases of different types
Synchronous and asynchronous replication are simply two names for the same mechanism
questions.explanation: The book notes synchronous replication "typically requires that the primary database and the replica are of the same type," while async CDC replication is a "loosely coupled architecture pattern" that can direct events to varied targets.

questions.question: When might a team consider a physical "transfer appliance" (like AWS Snowball) instead of transferring data over the internet?
options: For very large data volumes (roughly 100TB or more), physically shipping storage hardware can be faster and cheaper than internet transfer, especially given egress costs
Transfer appliances are recommended for all ongoing, continuous ingestion workloads regardless of size
They are legally required for any dataset that contains personally identifiable information
They eliminate the need for any further data ingestion pipeline going forward
questions.explanation: The book states: "For massive quantities of data (100 TB or more), transferring data directly over the internet may be a slow and costly process," recommending appliances at that scale, but not for ongoing workloads.

questions.question: What does the book mean by "touchless production" when handling sensitive data, and why is it an ideal worth striving for?
options: Engineers develop and test on simulated or cleansed data in dev/staging, with automated deployments to production — minimizing direct human handling of live sensitive data
It means production systems should never be monitored by any human at any time
It means sensitive data should be duplicated across every environment for consistency
It means production access should be granted permanently to the entire team for convenience
questions.explanation: The book defines it exactly this way: engineers "develop and test code on simulated or cleansed data in development and staging environments but automated code deployments to production."

questions.question: The book suggests asking "do you need the sensitive data you're trying to encrypt?" before building elaborate encryption schemes. What's the underlying principle?
options: Data that's never collected in the first place can't leak — dropping unnecessary sensitive fields at ingestion is often better than adding technical protections around data you didn't need to keep
Encryption is always unnecessary, since cloud storage is inherently secure by default
Data engineers should never be permitted to touch sensitive data under any policy
Tokenization should always be applied even to fields that aren't sensitive, for consistency
questions.explanation: The book states plainly: "Why not simply drop sensitive fields before data is stored? Data cannot leak if it is never collected."

questions.question: What does the book recommend monitoring specifically at the ingestion stage, and why is monitoring especially critical there?
options: Uptime, latency, and data volumes processed — ingestion sits at the start of the pipeline, so an undetected failure there silently starves every downstream stage of fresh data
Only the CPU temperature of the ingestion servers, per the book's guidance
Monitoring is described as unnecessary once a managed connector is in use
The book recommends monitoring only successful runs, never failures
questions.explanation: The book states: "Uptime, latency, and data volumes processed are good places to start," and cites a real example where "an ingestion pipeline failure wasn't detected for six months" due to weak monitoring.

questions.question: How does the book define bounded versus unbounded data?
options: Unbounded data is data as it exists in reality — events happening sporadically or continuously, ongoing and flowing; bounded data is a convenient way of bucketing data across some boundary such as time
Bounded data is data that cannot be moved; unbounded data can be moved freely
Unbounded data refers only to video and audio streams
Bounded data is always more accurate than unbounded data
questions.explanation: The book defines unbounded as data in reality and bounded as a convenient bucketing across a boundary such as time.

questions.question: How does the book acknowledge that the mantra "all data is unbounded until it's bounded" is not precisely accurate 100% of the time?
options: A grocery list scribbled this afternoon is bounded data, even though it started as a stream of consciousness — but the idea is correct for practical purposes for the vast majority of business data
It is 100% accurate with no exceptions
Bounded data never exists in any form
Only digital data can be bounded
questions.explanation: The book uses the grocery-list example to show a true bounded dataset, while noting the mantra holds for the vast majority of business data.

questions.question: What range of ingestion frequencies does the book describe?
options: From a business shipping tax data to an accounting firm once a year, to a CDC system retrieving log updates once a minute, to continuously ingesting IoT sensor events processed within seconds
All ingestion happens on a fixed daily schedule
Frequencies range only from seconds to minutes
Ingestion frequency is irrelevant to pipeline design
questions.explanation: The book describes this spectrum from slow (once a year) to fast (continuous seconds), noting frequencies are often mixed in a company.

questions.question: Even with streaming ingestion, why does the book say batch processing downstream remains relatively standard?
options: ML models are typically trained on a batch basis and rarely can engineers build a purely near real-time pipeline with no batch components — they choose where batch boundaries occur, and batch frequency becomes a bottleneck for downstream processing
Streaming ingestion always produces batched output automatically
Batch processing downstream is forbidden
Batch processing is never needed once streaming is used
questions.explanation: The book says batch processing downstream is standard, ML training is typically batch, and engineers choose where batch boundaries occur.

questions.question: Why does the book say streaming systems are the best fit for many data source types, such as IoT sensors?
options: The typical pattern is for each sensor to write events or measurements to streaming systems as they happen, which suits event-driven architectures already exchanging messages through queues
IoT sensors cannot write to any system
Streaming systems are required by law for IoT
Databases cannot store IoT data
questions.explanation: The book says sensors writing events to streaming platforms like Kinesis or Kafka is the typical pattern, working well for event-driven architectures.

questions.question: What are the characteristics of synchronous ingestion?
options: Source, ingestion, and destination have complex dependencies and are tightly coupled, with each stage directly dependent on the previous — if one stage fails, downstream stages cannot start and the whole process must be rerun
Each stage operates independently on individual events
Stages can all run in parallel with no dependencies
Failures are isolated to a single stage
questions.explanation: The book describes synchronous ingestion as tightly coupled dependent stages, common in older ETL systems, where failure of one stage blocks downstream stages.

questions.question: What is asynchronous ingestion, and how does it relate to microservices architectures?
options: Dependencies operate at the level of individual events, much as they would in a software backend built from microservices — each stage of the pipeline can process data items as they become available in parallel
It requires all events to be processed in a single batch
It only works with legacy mainframe systems
It cannot process individual events
questions.explanation: The book says with asynchronous ingestion "dependencies can now operate at the level of individual events," processing data items in parallel across a cluster.

questions.question: What AWS example does the book give of asynchronous ingestion, and what role does Kinesis play?
options: A web app emits events into Kinesis Data Streams (a buffer), Apache Beam parses and enriches them, forwarding to a second Kinesis stream, and Kinesis Data Firehose writes objects to S3; the Kinesis Data Stream acts as a shock absorber moderating load spikes
A database directly streams into S3 with no buffer
Kinesis is only used for batch processing
Beam replaces all storage and queues
questions.explanation: The book describes this exact asynchronous AWS architecture, highlighting Kinesis as a shock absorber.

questions.question: What advice does the book give about serialization and deserialization during ingestion?
options: Ensure your destination can deserialize the data it receives — data has been seen ingested from a source but sitting inert and unusable because it can't be deserialized
Serialization is irrelevant during ingestion
All data should be stored in its raw format regardless of the destination
Deserialization happens automatically with no failures
questions.explanation: The book says to ensure the destination can deserialize received data, citing the example of inert unusable data.

questions.question: What does the book say about ingestion as a bottleneck, and what should engineers do about throughput?
options: In theory ingestion should never be a bottleneck, but in practice bottlenecks are pretty standard; design systems to scale and shrink flexibly to match desired data throughput as volumes grow
Ingestion can never become a bottleneck
Throughput is fixed and cannot be scaled
Bottlenecks only occur in batch systems, never streaming
questions.explanation: The book says in theory ingestion shouldn't bottleneck but in practice it does, so design for flexible scaling.

questions.question: What backfill concern does the book raise about where you're ingesting data from?
options: If a source database goes down and later backfills lapsed data loads, your ingestion must be able to keep up with the sudden influx of backlogged data
Source databases never go down
Backfilled data is automatically discarded
Backlog always flows at a constant rate
questions.explanation: The book asks whether ingestion can keep up with a sudden influx of backlogged data after a source recovers.

questions.question: Why is built-in buffering required for bursty data ingestion?
options: Data generation rarely happens at a constant rate and often ebbs and flows; buffering collects events during rate spikes to prevent data loss and bridges the time while the system scales
Data always arrives at a perfectly constant rate
Buffering always increases data loss
Buffering is only needed for batch systems
questions.explanation: The book says buffering is required to collect events during rate spikes and allow storage to accommodate bursts.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about throughput scaling of ingestion systems?
options: Whenever possible, use managed services that handle throughput scaling for you, since manually adding servers, shards, or workers is often not value-added and you'll likely miss something
Always build your own scaling infrastructure
Never use managed services
Throughput scaling is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book recommends managed services for throughput scaling and warns against reinventing the ingestion wheel.

questions.question: How does the book define reliability and durability in the context of ingestion?
options: Reliability entails high uptime and proper failover for ingestion systems; durability entails making sure data isn't lost or corrupted
Reliability means only the destination is monitored
Durability means data can be freely deleted
They are identical concepts with no distinction
questions.explanation: The book defines reliability as uptime/failover and durability as preventing data loss or corruption.

questions.question: Why does the book say some data sources make ingestion reliability directly lead to data durability?
options: Some sources (e.g. IoT devices and caches) may not retain data if it isn't correctly ingested — once lost, it is gone for good
All sources retain data indefinitely
Lost data is always recoverable
Caches never lose data
questions.explanation: The book says IoT devices and caches may not retain data, so ingestion reliability leads directly to the durability of generated data.

questions.question: What does the book advise about the cost-benefit of reliability and durability decisions?
options: Evaluate the risks and build an appropriate level of redundancy and self-healing based on the impact and cost of losing data — high redundancy and 24-hour on-call teams make cloud and labor costs prohibitive, and there's no single correct answer
Build maximum redundancy with unlimited budget
Ignore costs entirely
There is one correct answer for every organization
questions.explanation: The book says to evaluate risk versus cost, noting the direct and indirect costs of high redundancy and that no single correct answer exists.

questions.question: Why does the book caution against assuming you can build a system that reliably ingests data in every possible scenario?
options: Even the nearly infinite budget of the US federal government can't guarantee this; in many extreme scenarios ingesting data won't matter, such as if the internet goes down entirely
Every scenario can be perfectly handled with enough money
The internet never goes down
Reliability guarantees are easy to provide
questions.explanation: The book uses the federal government budget example and notes there will be little to ingest if the internet goes down.

questions.question: What is a payload, and what characteristics does the book list for it?
options: The dataset you're ingesting, with characteristics such as kind, shape, size, schema and data types, and metadata
The physical hardware used for transfer
The network bandwidth consumed during transfer
The orchestration schedule of the pipeline
questions.explanation: The book defines a payload as the dataset being ingested with characteristics of kind, shape, size, schema/data types, and metadata.

questions.question: What does "kind" of data consist of, and what examples does the book give?
options: Kind consists of type and format — a tabular type may be in formats such as CSV or Parquet with different byte patterns, while an image type has formats like JPG or PNG and is inherently unstructured
Kind refers only to the file extension
Kind means the physical storage medium
Kind describes how often data is ingested
questions.explanation: The book says kind consists of type and format, with tabular (CSV/Parquet) and image (JPG/PNG) examples.

questions.question: What shapes does the book list for various kinds of data?
options: Tabular as rows/columns, semistructured JSON as key-value pairs and nesting depth, unstructured text as word/character/byte counts, images as width/height/RGB color depth, and audio as channels, sample depth, sample rate, and length
All data has the same shape
Shape only applies to images
Shape is determined by the network protocol
questions.explanation: The book lists these shape descriptions for each kind of data.

questions.question: How does the book say payload size can be reduced, and how can a massive payload be moved?
options: Payloads can be compressed into formats such as ZIP and TAR, and a massive payload can be split into chunks — smaller files are easier to transmit over a network and reassembled at the destination
Payloads cannot be compressed or chunked
Compression always increases payload size
Chunking makes transmission slower
questions.explanation: The book says payloads can be compressed (ZIP/TAR) and split into chunks that are transmitted and reassembled.

questions.question: What does the book say about schemas across different kinds of data?
options: Tabular and semistructured data have schemas describing fields and types, while unstructured text, images, and audio have no explicit schema but may come with technical file descriptions on shape, format, encoding, and size
All data types have explicit schemas
Only images have schemas
Schemas never describe fields or types
questions.explanation: The book distinguishes schema-carrying data from unstructured data with technical descriptions.

questions.question: What complication does the book describe regarding object-relational mapping (ORM) and schemas?
options: ORMs automatically generate schemas based on object structure in languages like Java or Python, and natural structures in an object-oriented language often map to something messy in an operational database, so engineers may need to familiarize themselves with the class structure of application code
ORMs eliminate the need for any schema understanding
ORMs always produce perfectly clean schemas
ORMs are only used in NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: The book says ORMs generate messy schemas and engineers may need to understand the application's class structure.

questions.question: What examples of schema changes does the book give, and why are they often out of engineers' control?
options: Adding a new column, changing a column type, creating a new table, or renaming a column — changes frequently occur in source systems and are often well out of data engineers' control
Schema changes only happen at the destination
Schema changes never occur in source systems
Only the data engineer can change schemas
questions.explanation: The book lists these schema change examples and notes they are often out of the data engineer's control.

questions.question: Why does the book call automated detection of schema changes a "mixed blessing"?
options: Automation is excellent, but schema changes can still break pipelines downstream of staging and ingestion, and even accommodated changes may adversely affect the performance of reports and models — so analysts and data scientists must be informed
Automation always breaks pipelines
Schema changes never affect reports or models
Automation eliminates the need for any communication
questions.explanation: The book says automated schema-change detection is a mixed blessing because changes can still break pipelines and hurt reports/models, so communication is essential.

questions.question: What is a schema registry?
options: A metadata repository used to maintain schema and data type integrity in the face of constantly changing schemas, tracking schema versions and history so producers and consumers can serialize and deserialize consistently
A physical registry of all databases
A backup system for schema files
A queue for failed messages
questions.explanation: The book defines a schema registry as a metadata repository maintaining schema/data-type integrity with version history.

questions.question: Why does the book say metadata can be as critical as the data itself?
options: One significant limitation of the early data lake — or data swamp, which could become a data superfund site — was a complete lack of attention to metadata; without a detailed description of the data, it may be of little value
Metadata is only useful for billing
Data lakes never had metadata problems
Metadata makes data less valuable
questions.explanation: The book connects the data swamp problem to a lack of metadata and says without a description data may be of little value.

questions.question: How does the book distinguish push, pull, and polling ingestion patterns?
options: Push has the source system send data to a target; pull has the target read data directly from a source; polling periodically checks a source for changes and then pulls the data as in a regular pull
Push and pull are identical
Polling only applies to batch systems
Push requires the target to initiate
questions.explanation: The book defines push, pull, and polling patterns, noting the lines between strategies are blurry.

questions.question: What is time-interval batch ingestion, and where is it widespread?
options: Data is ingested by taking a subset based on a time interval — widespread in traditional business ETL for data warehousing, often processing data once a day overnight for daily reporting
Data is ingested only when a customer calls
It is used only for IoT sensor data
It processes data continuously with no intervals
questions.explanation: The book says time-interval batch ingestion is widespread in traditional business ETL for data warehousing, typically daily overnight.

questions.question: What is size-based batch ingestion, and where is it common?
options: Data is cut into discrete blocks based on accumulated size (e.g. total bytes of events) — quite common when moving data from a streaming-based system into object storage for future processing in a data lake
Data is ingested one event at a time regardless of size
It only applies to on-premises tapes
Size never determines batch boundaries
questions.explanation: The book says size-based batch ingestion is common when moving streaming data into object storage, breaking data into discrete blocks.

questions.question: Why do full snapshot reads remain extremely common even though differential updates are more efficient?
options: Differential updates are ideal for minimizing network traffic and target storage usage, but full snapshot reads remain extremely common because of their simplicity
Full snapshots use less storage than differential updates
Differential updates are always slower
Full snapshots reduce network traffic more effectively
questions.explanation: The book says full snapshots remain common because of simplicity despite differential updates minimizing traffic and storage.

questions.question: Why does the book consider file-based export to be a push-based ingestion pattern?
options: Data export and preparation work is done on the source system side, so the source drives the process
The target system pulls files from the source
File export always requires polling
Files are never used for ingestion
questions.explanation: The book says file-based export is a push-based pattern because data export and preparation happens on the source side.

questions.question: What common file-exchange methods does the book list?
options: Object storage, secure file transfer protocol (SFTP), electronic data interchange (EDI), and secure copy (SCP)
Only email attachments
Only USB flash drives
Only direct database connections
questions.explanation: The book lists object storage, SFTP, EDI, and SCP as common file-exchange methods.

questions.question: How does the book define "extract" in the ETL/ELT context?
options: Getting data from a source system — while extract seems to imply pulling, it can also be push based, and it may require reading metadata and schema changes
Only pulling data from databases
Transforming data into a new format
Loading data into a destination
questions.explanation: The book says extract means getting data from a source, can be push or pull, and may involve reading metadata and schema changes.

questions.question: What does the book say about the "load" step in ETL and ELT?
options: Once extracted, data can either be transformed (ETL) before loading into a storage destination, or simply loaded into storage for future transformation (ELT); when loading, be mindful of the system type, the data schema, and the performance impact
Loading always happens before extraction
Load only applies to ELT, never ETL
Schema and performance never matter when loading
questions.explanation: The book defines load and its considerations of system type, schema, and performance impact.

questions.question: What does the book say about BigQuery's performance on different insert patterns?
options: BigQuery performs poorly on a high rate of vanilla SQL single-row inserts but extremely well if data is fed in through its stream buffer
BigQuery handles single-row inserts perfectly
BigQuery cannot ingest any data
BigQuery only works with batch loads
questions.explanation: The book contrasts BigQuery's poor single-row insert performance with excellent stream-buffer performance.

questions.question: Which technologies does the book cite as purpose-built for high insert rates, and what does SingleStore offer?
options: Apache Druid and Apache Pinot can handle high insert rates; SingleStore can manage hybrid workloads that combine OLAP and OLTP characteristics
Only traditional RDBMSs handle high insert rates
SingleStore is a columnar-only analytics system
Druid and Pinot cannot handle inserts
questions.explanation: The book names Druid and Pinot for high insert rates and SingleStore for hybrid OLAP/OLTP workloads.

questions.question: What does the book say about data migration difficulty and schema management?
options: Migrating hundreds of terabytes or more between different database systems involves subtle schema differences (e.g. SQL Server to Snowflake), and it's generally easy to test ingestion of a sample of data to find schema issues before undertaking a complete migration
Migrations are always trivial
Schema differences never matter between databases
Testing sample data before migration is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book says schema management is crucial in migrations and sample testing finds schema issues before full migration.

questions.question: What does the book say is one of the biggest challenges of database migration?
options: Not the movement of the data itself, but the movement of data pipeline connections from the old system to the new one
The physical shipment of hard drives
The cost of cloud storage
The network bandwidth during transfer
questions.explanation: The book says the biggest challenge is moving data pipeline connections, not the data itself.

questions.question: What advice does the book give about automated data migration tools?
options: Many tools automate various types of data migrations, and especially for large and complex migrations you should look at these options before doing this manually or writing your own migration solution
Always write your own migration code
Automated migration tools never work
Manual migration is always better
questions.explanation: The book recommends looking at automated migration tools before manual or custom solutions for large migrations.

questions.question: What examples does the book give of schema evolution in event data, and how can it impact downstream capabilities?
options: An IoT device firmware update that adds a new field to transmitted events, or a third-party API introducing changes to its event payload — both potentially impact downstream capabilities
Event schemas never change
Only database tables have schemas
Schema evolution has no downstream impact
questions.explanation: The book gives the IoT firmware and third-party API examples of schema evolution's downstream impacts.

questions.question: What three suggestions does the book make for alleviating schema evolution issues in event processing?
options: Use a schema registry to version schema changes, use a dead-letter queue to investigate improperly handled events, and regularly communicate with upstream stakeholders about potential schema changes
Ignore schema changes entirely
Only react to schema changes after breakage
Reject all events with new schemas
questions.explanation: The book lists the schema registry, dead-letter queue, and proactive communication as the three suggestions.

questions.question: How does the book say to handle late-arriving data?
options: Set a cutoff time for when late-arriving data will no longer be processed, since assuming ingestion time equals event time can produce strange results in reports and analysis
Ignore late-arriving data entirely
Assume all data arrives on time
Process late-arriving data indefinitely without limits
questions.explanation: The book says to set a cutoff time for late-arriving data, which is common in event ingestion.

questions.question: What is time to live (TTL), and what does the book say happens when it expires?
options: The maximum message retention time; any unacknowledged event not ingested after its TTL expires automatically disappears, which helps reduce backpressure and unnecessary event volume
The amount of time a message stays in the destination
The total lifetime of the ingestion system
The delay before the first message is processed
questions.explanation: The book defines TTL as maximum message retention and says unacknowledged events disappear when it expires, reducing backpressure.

questions.question: What trade-offs does the book describe for very short versus very long TTLs?
options: An extremely short TTL (milliseconds or seconds) might cause most messages to disappear before processing; a very long TTL (weeks or months) creates a backlog of unprocessed messages and long wait times
Shorter TTLs always improve processing
Longer TTLs always reduce backlogs
TTL has no effect on the pipeline
questions.explanation: The book describes both extremes: messages vanishing with short TTLs and backlogs with long TTLs.

questions.question: What TTL/retention limits does the book cite for Pub/Sub, Kinesis, and Kafka?
options: Pub/Sub supports retention up to 7 days; Kinesis Data Streams up to 365 days; Kafka can be configured for indefinite retention limited by available disk space, and can write older messages to cloud object storage
All platforms have the same 7-day limit
Kafka cannot retain data at all
Kinesis retention is limited to 1 day
questions.explanation: The book cites these specific retention limits for the three platforms.

questions.question: What does the book say about message size limits in streaming frameworks?
options: You must ensure the framework can handle the maximum expected message size — Amazon Kinesis supports a maximum of 1 MB, and Kafka defaults to this but can be configured for 20 MB or more
Message size is unlimited in all frameworks
Kinesis supports messages up to 20 MB
Kafka cannot exceed 1 MB under any configuration
questions.explanation: The book cites Kinesis's 1 MB max and Kafka's configurable 20 MB+ maximum.

questions.question: What does a dead-letter queue do for a consumer, and what can engineers do with it?
options: It segregates problematic events from events that can be accepted, preventing erroneous events from blocking other messages; engineers can diagnose why ingestion errors occur and might reprocess some messages after fixing the underlying cause
It stores all successfully processed events
It is the main processing queue
It automatically deletes problematic events
questions.explanation: The book says a dead-letter queue segregates bad events, enables diagnosis, and allows reprocessing after fixes.

questions.question: Which streaming technologies support only pull subscriptions, and which also support push?
options: Kafka and Kinesis support only pull subscriptions; Pub/Sub and RabbitMQ also support push subscriptions that write messages to a listener
All platforms support only push
RabbitMQ supports only pull
Kafka supports both push and pull
questions.explanation: The book says Kafka and Kinesis are pull-only, while Pub/Sub and RabbitMQ add push subscriptions.

questions.question: What does the book say about the default choice between pull and push subscriptions for data engineering?
options: Pull subscriptions are the default choice for most data engineering applications, but push capabilities may be worth considering for specialized applications; pull-only systems can still push if you add an extra layer
Push subscriptions are always preferred
Pull is never used in data engineering
The choice makes no difference
questions.explanation: The book says pull is the default, with push for specialized applications and an extra layer enabling push in pull-only systems.

questions.question: What trade-off does the book describe about ingesting data close to where it originates?
options: The closer your ingestion is to where data originates, the better your bandwidth and latency, but you must balance this against the costs of moving data between regions for combined analytics, since data egress costs can spiral quickly
Closer ingestion is always more expensive
Location has no effect on latency or cost
Egress costs never matter
questions.explanation: The book describes the bandwidth/latency benefit of proximity balanced against region-crossing egress costs.

questions.question: How does the book describe the ODBC connection mechanism?
options: A driver hosted by the client translates commands issued to the standard ODBC API into commands to the database; the database returns query results over the wire and the driver translates them back to a standard form the client reads
The database pushes data to the client without any driver
ODBC requires a dedicated appliance
ODBC only works with NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: The book describes the ODBC driver's translation between the standard API and the database.

questions.question: How is JDBC conceptually similar to ODBC, and what motivation does the book give for a language-specific database API?
options: A Java driver connects to a remote database and serves as a translation layer between the JDBC API and the database's native interface; the JVM is standard, portable across hardware and OS, and provides compiled-code performance through a just-in-time (JIT) compiler
JDBC does not use a driver at all
The JVM is not portable
JDBC only works on Windows
questions.explanation: The book describes JDBC's translation layer and the JVM's portability and JIT performance motivations.

questions.question: What portability advantage does JDBC offer over ODBC?
options: ODBC drivers are shipped as OS/architecture native binaries requiring vendor maintenance per version, while vendors can ship a single JDBC driver compatible with any JVM language or JVM data framework such as Spark, and even non-JVM languages like Python via translation tools
JDBC drivers must be rebuilt for every OS
ODBC is more portable than JDBC
JDBC only works with Java, never Spark
questions.explanation: The book contrasts ODBC's native-binary shipping with JDBC's single-driver portability across JVM languages, frameworks, and Python.

questions.question: What does the book say about using parallel connections to accelerate JDBC/ODBC ingestion?
options: Many data frameworks can parallelize several simultaneous connections and partition queries to pull data in parallel, but nothing is free — parallel connections also increase the load on the source database
Parallel connections reduce source database load
Parallel queries are never used
Partitioning queries has no effect on the source
questions.explanation: The book notes the acceleration benefit and the increased source-load cost of parallel connections.

questions.question: What alternatives to JDBC/ODBC for data export does the book describe?
options: Many databases now support native file export that bypasses JDBC/ODBC and exports directly in formats such as Parquet, ORC, and Avro, and many cloud data warehouses provide direct REST APIs
JDBC/ODBC are the only export options
Native export only works for images
REST APIs cannot export data
questions.explanation: The book describes native file export and direct REST APIs as alternatives to JDBC/ODBC.

questions.question: How does the book suggest JDBC connections be integrated with other ingestion technologies?
options: Use a reader process to connect to a database with JDBC, write the extracted data into multiple objects, and then orchestrate ingestion into a downstream system; the reader can run on an ephemeral cloud instance or in an orchestration system
JDBC should always be used alone
Reader processes cannot write objects
Orchestration never interacts with JDBC ingestion
questions.explanation: The book describes the reader-process-to-object-storage-then-orchestration pattern.

questions.question: How does batch-oriented CDC work with an updated_at field?
options: Query the table for all updated rows since a specified time, setting the filter timestamp based on when rows were last captured, to pull changes and differentially update a target table
It deletes the whole table and reloads it
It reads the entire database every time
It requires the target to push changes
questions.explanation: The book describes querying by updated_at since the last capture to differentially update the target.

questions.question: How can the bank-withdrawal limitation of batch CDC be mitigated?
options: By utilizing an insert-only schema, where each account transaction is recorded as a new record in the table rather than updating the balance in place
By running batch CDC more frequently with the same in-place updates
By disabling CDC entirely
By storing only the final balance
questions.explanation: The book says an insert-only schema records each transaction as a new record, mitigating the lost-intermediate-changes limitation.

questions.question: What is continuous CDC, and how is log-based CDC commonly implemented?
options: Continuous CDC treats each write to the database as an event, capturing all table history for near real-time ingestion; with a transactional database such as PostgreSQL, a CDC tool reads the database binary log and sends events to a target such as Apache Kafka's Debezium
Continuous CDC runs periodic queries
Log-based CDC cannot capture changes
PostgreSQL has no binary log
questions.explanation: The book describes continuous CDC as event-based, with log-based CDC reading the binary log, e.g. via Debezium to Kafka.

questions.question: What managed CDC paradigm does the book describe for cloud-hosted databases?
options: Many cloud-hosted databases can be configured to directly trigger a serverless function or write to an event stream every time a change happens, freeing engineers from worrying about how events are captured and forwarded
Cloud databases require manual log reading
Serverless functions cannot receive database events
Managed CDC does not exist
questions.explanation: The book describes managed cloud CDC that triggers serverless functions or writes to event streams on each change.

questions.question: What advantages does synchronous replication provide?
options: The secondary database can offload work from the primary by acting as a read replica, applications can fail over to it if the primary becomes unavailable with no data loss, and batch ingestion can run large scans against the replica without overloading production
It allows replication between different database types
It always lags behind the primary
It cannot support read replicas
questions.explanation: The book describes read-replica offloading, failover with no data loss, and safe large scans against replicas.

questions.question: What considerations does the book raise about CDC's resource consumption?
options: CDC consumes database resources such as memory, disk bandwidth, storage, CPU time, and network bandwidth, so engineers should work with production teams and run tests before turning on CDC on production systems
CDC is completely free of resource costs
CDC never affects production systems
Testing CDC before production is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book lists CDC's resource costs and recommends testing with production teams first.

questions.question: What does the book say about running large batch queries for batch CDC against a transactional production system?
options: Running any large batch query against a transactional production system can cause excessive load; run such queries only at off-hours or use a read replica to avoid burdening the primary database
Large batch queries never affect production
Batch queries should always run during peak hours
Read replicas increase production load
questions.explanation: The book advises off-hours queries or read replicas for large batch CDC queries.

questions.question: What hard reality does the book describe about APIs as a data source?
options: No proper standard exists for data exchange over APIs, and data engineers can spend significant time reading documentation, communicating with external data owners, and writing and maintaining API connection code
All APIs follow a universal standard
APIs never require custom code
API documentation is always complete
questions.explanation: The book says no proper API data-exchange standard exists and engineers spend significant time on API connections.

questions.question: What three trends does the book say are slowly changing the API situation?
options: Vendor API client libraries, data connector platforms available as SaaS/open source/managed open source, and the emergence of data sharing through standard platforms
The decline of APIs entirely
A single universal API standard
Automated API documentation
questions.explanation: The book lists client libraries, connector platforms, and data sharing as the three trends.

questions.question: What does the book say about managed services that support custom API connectors?
options: They may provide API technical specifications in a standard format or run connector code in a serverless function framework like AWS Lambda while the managed service handles scheduling and synchronization — a huge time-saver for development and maintenance
Managed services never support custom connectors
Custom connectors must always be fully self-managed
Serverless functions cannot run connector code
questions.explanation: The book describes managed custom-connector support and its time-saving benefits.

questions.question: What two main aspects does the book say handling custom API connections has, and what practices does it recommend?
options: Software development and ops — follow software development best practices such as version control, continuous delivery, and automated testing, and consider an orchestration framework to streamline the operational burden
Only hardware procurement
Only legal review
Only documentation writing
questions.explanation: The book says custom API work has software development and ops aspects with best-practice recommendations.

questions.question: How does the book contrast batch ingestion workflows with message/stream ingestion?
options: Batch usually involves static workflows (ingest, store, transform, serve), while messages and streams are fluid — ingestion can be nonlinear, with data published, consumed, republished, and reconsumed
Streaming workflows are always static
Batch workflows are always nonlinear
There is no difference between them
questions.explanation: The book describes the essential difference: static batch workflows versus fluid, nonlinear streaming.

questions.question: What throughput considerations does the book raise for real-time data pipelines?
options: Provision adequate partition (or shard) bandwidth and throughput, provide sufficient memory/disk/CPU for event processing, and incorporate autoscaling to handle spikes and save money as load decreases
Provisioning has no effect on real-time pipelines
Autoscaling is never recommended
Only CPU resources matter
questions.explanation: The book lists partition/shard bandwidth, resources, and autoscaling for real-time pipelines.

questions.question: What should you ask yourself before writing a data ingestion connector, per the book?
options: Has this already been created? And is there a service that will manage the nitty-gritty details of this connection for me?
What language should I use?
Which server should host it?
How many lines of code can I write?
questions.explanation: The book recommends asking whether the connector already exists and whether a service can manage the connection.

questions.question: What options do managed data connector platforms generally allow users to set?
options: Set a target and source, ingest in various ways (e.g. CDC, replication, truncate and reload), set permissions and credentials, configure an update frequency, and begin syncing — with the vendor fully managing and monitoring data syncs
Only the target database
Only the sync frequency
Nothing — connections are automatic
questions.explanation: The book describes the configuration options and vendor-managed monitoring of connector platforms.

questions.question: Why does the book recommend using managed connector platforms instead of creating your own?
options: Vendors and OSS projects each typically have hundreds of prebuilt connectors and can easily create custom ones; the creation and management of data connectors is largely undifferentiated heavy lifting that should be outsourced whenever possible
Custom connectors are always better
Managed platforms have no prebuilt connectors
Connector creation is high-value differentiated work
questions.explanation: The book calls connector creation and management undifferentiated heavy lifting to outsource.

questions.question: Why does the book say object storage is the most optimal and secure way to handle file exchange?
options: Public cloud storage implements the latest security standards, has a robust track record of scalability and reliability, accepts files of arbitrary types and sizes, and provides high-performance data movement
Object storage is only used for backups
Object storage rejects most file types
Object storage is insecure by default
questions.explanation: The book lists security, scalability, reliability, arbitrary files, and high-performance movement as reasons.

questions.question: What is a signed URL in object storage, and what does it allow?
options: A way to provide short-term access to an object, giving a user temporary permission
A permanent credential for every user
An encrypted backup of an object
A URL that never expires
questions.explanation: The book says a signed URL provides short-term temporary access to an object.

questions.question: What does the book say about electronic data interchange (EDI)?
options: It's a vague term for any data movement method, usually referring to somewhat archaic means of file exchange such as email or flash drive, often because of archaic IT systems or human process limitations
It is a modern high-speed protocol
It only refers to object storage
It is a type of database
questions.explanation: The book describes EDI as a vague, often archaic file-exchange term.

questions.question: How can engineers enhance EDI through automation?
options: Set up a cloud-based email server that saves files onto company object storage as soon as they are received, triggering orchestration processes to ingest and process data
EDI cannot be automated
Employees must manually download and upload files
Orchestration cannot process object storage files
questions.explanation: The book describes automated EDI via a cloud email server saving to object storage and triggering orchestration.

questions.question: What load concern does the book raise about file export from source databases, and what mitigations does it suggest?
options: Export involves large data scans that significantly load transactional systems; break exports into smaller queries over key ranges or one partition at a time, or use a read replica, especially if exports happen many times a day
Exports never load the source database
Exports should always run during peak hours
Read replicas increase export load
questions.explanation: The book suggests key-range/partitioned exports and read replicas to mitigate export load.

questions.question: What does the book say about direct file export from major cloud data warehouses?
options: They are highly optimized for direct file export — for example, Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, and others support direct export to object storage in various formats
Cloud warehouses cannot export files
Only on-premises systems support export
Export is limited to CSV only
questions.explanation: The book says cloud warehouses like Snowflake, BigQuery, and Redshift support direct export to object storage.

questions.question: Why does the book describe CSV as ubiquitous but highly error prone?
options: Its default delimiter is the comma (familiar in English text), it is by no means a uniform format requiring stipulation of delimiter/quote/escaping, doesn't natively encode schema information, and doesn't directly support nested structures
CSV cannot be read by any tool
CSV always encodes schemas natively
CSV supports nested structures natively
questions.explanation: The book describes CSV's delimiter ambiguity, non-uniformity, and lack of schema/nesting support.

questions.question: Why is autodetection of CSV encoding/schema inappropriate for production ingestion?
options: Autodetection is a convenience feature in many cloud environments but is inappropriate for production ingestion; engineers should record CSV encoding and schema details in file metadata as a best practice
Autodetection is always perfectly accurate
Autodetection is recommended for production
CSV metadata is never useful
questions.explanation: The book recommends recording CSV encoding/schema details in metadata rather than relying on autodetection in production.

questions.question: What advantages do formats like Parquet, Avro, Arrow, and ORC offer over CSV?
options: They natively encode schema information, handle arbitrary string data with no particular intervention, handle nested data structures natively, and for columnar databases allow more efficient export via direct column transcoding
They are always smaller than CSV
They cannot store string data
They require more manual schema configuration
questions.explanation: The book describes these formats' native schema encoding, nested-structure support, and efficient columnar transcoding.

questions.question: What is special about the Arrow file format according to the book?
options: It is designed to map data directly into processing engine memory, providing high performance in data lake environments
It can only be used for images
It is the slowest format available
It requires manual memory management
questions.explanation: The book says Arrow maps data directly into processing engine memory for high performance.

questions.question: What disadvantage do newer formats like Parquet, Avro, and Arrow have?
options: Many are not natively supported by source systems, so engineers are often forced to work with CSV and build robust exception handling and error detection to ensure data quality on ingestion
They are slower than CSV
They cannot be used for ingestion
They are all proprietary
questions.explanation: The book says newer formats often lack native source-system support, leaving CSV with added error handling.

questions.question: What does the book say about using the shell for ingestion?
options: The shell can script workflows for virtually any software tool, and shell scripting is still used extensively; a script might read from a database, reserialize to another format, upload to object storage, and trigger a target ingestion — fine for sources that aren't large since single-server storage isn't highly scalable
Shell scripting cannot ingest data
Shell is only for batch processing
Shell scripts are never used in ingestion
questions.explanation: The book describes shell-based ingestion workflows and their suitability for smaller sources.

questions.question: When should engineers move from CLI-based ingestion to a proper orchestration system?
options: As ingestion processes grow more complicated and the SLA grows more stringent, engineers should consider moving to a proper orchestration system
Never — CLI tools are always sufficient
Only when the cloud provider requires it
CLI tools cannot run ingestion at all
questions.explanation: The book says growing complexity and stringent SLAs warrant a proper orchestration system.

questions.question: How does the book characterize SSH in the context of ingestion?
options: SSH is not an ingestion strategy but a protocol used with other ingestion strategies — for file transfer with SCP and for SSH tunnels providing secure, isolated connections to databases
SSH is the main ingestion strategy
SSH cannot transfer files
SSH tunnels expose databases to the internet
questions.explanation: The book says SSH is a protocol supporting other strategies, via SCP and tunnels.

questions.question: What is a bastion host, and how is it used?
options: An intermediate host instance that can connect to a database; it is exposed on the internet but locked down to minimal access from specified IP addresses and ports, with remote machines opening an SSH tunnel to it before connecting to the database
A server that hosts the database directly on the internet
A host that never connects to databases
A firewall that blocks all database access
questions.explanation: The book describes the bastion host pattern for securely accessing application databases.

questions.question: What does the book say about SFTP and SCP as practical ingestion realities?
options: They are techniques engineers should be familiar with even if not used regularly; SFTP remains a practical reality with partners, requiring security analysis to avoid data leaks, and SCP runs over SSH with network access control (defense in depth) recommended
SFTP and SCP are always insecure
They are never used in business
SCP does not use SSH
questions.explanation: The book describes SFTP/SCP familiarity, security analysis, and defense-in-depth recommendations.

questions.question: How does a webhook differ from a typical REST API call?
options: With a webhook the data provider defines the API request specification but the provider makes the API calls rather than receiving them; it's the data consumer's responsibility to provide an API endpoint for the provider to call
Webhooks are identical to REST APIs
The consumer makes requests to the provider
Webhooks do not use HTTP
questions.explanation: The book explains webhooks as the reverse of typical APIs, with the provider calling the consumer's endpoint.

questions.question: What robust webhook architecture does the book describe for AWS?
options: A serverless function framework (Lambda) to receive incoming events, a managed event-streaming platform (Kinesis) to store and buffer messages, a stream-processing framework (Flink) for real-time analytics, and an object store (S3) for long-term storage
A single monolithic server
Lambda alone with no storage
Only on-premises hardware
questions.explanation: The book describes this AWS webhook architecture combining Lambda, Kinesis, Flink, and S3.

questions.question: What does the book say about webhook-based ingestion architectures and ingestion's entanglement with other lifecycle stages?
options: Webhook architectures can be brittle, difficult to maintain, and inefficient; the AWS architecture does much more than ingest, underscoring that it is often impossible to define your ingestion architecture without making decisions about storage and processing
Webhooks are always efficient
Ingestion can always be defined in isolation
Storage decisions never affect ingestion
questions.explanation: The book highlights webhook brittleness and ingestion's entanglement with storage and processing.

questions.question: What drawbacks does the book describe for web interface data access?
options: Someone must manually access the interface, generate a report, and download a file, with drawbacks such as people forgetting to run the report or their laptop dying; where possible, choose tools and workflows that allow automated access
Web interfaces are fully automated
Manual access has no drawbacks
Reports generate themselves
questions.explanation: The book describes manual web-interface drawbacks and recommends automated access.

questions.question: What is web scraping, and what ethical concern does the book raise?
options: Automatically extracting data from web pages, often by combing HTML elements — widespread, but a murky area where ethical and legal lines are blurry
A fully legal and unambiguous practice
A technique that only applies to APIs
A method for database backup
questions.explanation: The book defines web scraping and notes its blurry ethical and legal lines.

questions.question: What top-level advice does the book give before undertaking web scraping?
options: Ask whether you should scrape or whether data is available from a third party; if you scrape, be a good citizen — don't create a denial-of-service attack, don't get your IP blocked, and understand and pace the traffic you generate
Always scrape as aggressively as possible
Ignore the impact on target sites
Data is never available from third parties
questions.explanation: The book advises considering third-party data and being a good citizen to avoid DoS and IP blocks.

questions.question: What legal warnings does the book give about web scraping?
options: Generating DoS attacks can entail legal consequences, and actions that violate terms of service may cause headaches for your employer or you personally
Web scraping has no legal implications
Terms of service never matter
DoS attacks are always legal
questions.explanation: The book warns about legal consequences of DoS and terms-of-service violations.

questions.question: What maintenance challenge does the book describe for web scrapers?
options: Web pages constantly change their HTML element structure, making it tricky to keep the scraper updated — ask whether the headache of maintaining these systems is worth the effort
Web pages never change
Scrapers never need maintenance
HTML structure is stable forever
questions.explanation: The book describes the maintenance burden of HTML structure changes.

questions.question: What downstream architecture decision does the book say web scraping presents?
options: Whether to pull only required fields from the scraped HTML with Python and write values to a database, or maintain the complete HTML and process it with a framework like Spark — decisions leading to very different architectures downstream of ingestion
Scraping never affects downstream architecture
All scraped data must be discarded
There is only one valid scraping pipeline
questions.explanation: The book describes the field-only versus full-HTML processing decision and its architectural implications.

questions.question: What does the book say about AWS's Snowmobile transfer appliance?
options: It is a transfer appliance sent to you in a semitrailer, intended to lift and shift an entire data center, with data sizes in the petabytes or greater
It is a small portable drive
It is a standard cloud storage service
It transfers data over the internet
questions.explanation: The book describes Snowmobile as a semitrailer-sized appliance for petabyte-scale data center moves.

questions.question: How are transfer appliances useful for hybrid-cloud or multicloud setups?
options: AWS Snowball supports import and export, so users can export data into a Snowball and import it into a second transfer appliance to move data into GCP or Azure, which is often cheaper than pushing data over the internet due to data egress fees
Transfer appliances only work within one cloud
Egress fees never make internet transfer costly
Snowball cannot export data
questions.explanation: The book describes using Snowball for cloud-to-cloud migration as a cheaper alternative to internet transfer.

questions.question: Why are transfer appliances not suggested for ongoing workloads?
options: Transfer appliances and data migration services are one-time data ingestion events; ongoing workloads should batch or stream much smaller data sizes on a continuing basis
They are ideal for constant data movement
They are cheaper than streaming for small data
They should be used for every sync
questions.explanation: The book says transfer appliances are one-time events, not for ongoing workloads.

questions.question: How does data sharing as a consumption option differ from true ingestion?
options: Datasets are often shared read-only — you can integrate them with your own data but do not own them, and if the provider removes your access you no longer have access; this isn't ingestion where you get physical possession of the dataset
Data sharing always transfers full ownership
Shared datasets are always free to keep forever
Data sharing is identical to ingestion
questions.explanation: The book contrasts read-only data sharing with ingestion's physical possession.

questions.question: What does the book say about the disconnect between software engineers and data engineers?
options: They usually sit in separate organizational silos; software engineers typically see data engineers as downstream consumers of data exhaust from their application, not as stakeholders
They always work in the same team
Software engineers never generate data
There is no disconnect
questions.explanation: The book describes the siloed view of data engineers as mere downstream consumers.

questions.question: How can data engineers improve data quality by engaging software engineers?
options: Invite software engineers to be stakeholders in data engineering outcomes; most are aware of analytics/data science value but don't have aligned incentives to contribute directly, so opening a communication channel encourages them to get data into shape and communicate about changes
Software engineers should be excluded from data work
Communication makes quality worse
Software engineers have no useful data knowledge
questions.explanation: The book recommends making software engineers stakeholders and opening communication channels.

questions.question: How does the book suggest involving product managers and executives in data engineering?
options: Highlight software engineers' contributions to team members, executives, and especially product managers; involving product managers in outcomes encourages them to allocate software development to collaboration, and data engineers can provide executives guidance on structuring a data-driven business
Keep all data work invisible to executives
Product managers should never be involved
Executives need no guidance on data culture
questions.explanation: The book recommends highlighting contributions and involving product managers and executives.

questions.question: Who are the ultimate customers for data ingestion, and why should engineers remember a broader business circle?
options: Data practitioners and technology leaders such as data scientists, analysts, and CTOs, but also a broader circle such as marketing directors, supply-chain VPs, and CEOs — because basic automation of ingestion for departments like marketing can open up more budget and opportunities
Only the CTO
Only data scientists
Executives never consume data
questions.explanation: The book says to view data engineering as a business and recognize all customers, including marketing.

questions.question: What security considerations does the book raise for moving data between locations?
options: Data within your VPC should use secure endpoints and never leave the VPC; use a VPN or dedicated private connection between cloud and on-premises; and if data traverses the public internet, ensure the transmission is encrypted
Encryption is unnecessary for data movement
Data can always travel over the public internet unencrypted
VPCs and VPNs are not security measures
questions.explanation: The book lists VPC endpoints, VPN/private connections, and encryption over the wire as security measures.

questions.question: Why does the book say data management begins at data ingestion?
options: This is the starting point for lineage and data cataloging; from this point on, data engineers need to think about schema changes, ethics, privacy, and compliance
Data management only applies to storage
Ingestion has no relation to data management
Lineage begins at the data warehouse
questions.explanation: The book says data management begins at ingestion as the starting point for lineage and cataloging.

questions.question: What does the book say about the traditional command-and-control approach to schema changes?
options: It can involve lead times of six months for the addition of a single field at large enterprises, which is an unacceptable impediment to agility
It is the most agile approach
Schema changes never require review
Six-month lead times are ideal
questions.explanation: The book cites six-month lead times for a single field as unacceptable.

questions.question: What Git-inspired solution does the book describe for handling schema changes?
options: Since storage is cheap in big data and cloud environments, teams can maintain multiple versions of a table with different schemas and upstream transformations, using orchestration tools like Airflow so schema and code changes appear in development tables before official changes to the main table
A single official version like CVS
Centralized schema control
Deleting all old table versions
questions.explanation: The book draws on Git's distributed branch/tree model to propose multi-version tables.

questions.question: What does the book recommend about tokenization and hashing of sensitive identities?
options: Where it's necessary to track sensitive identities, tokenization is common to anonymize identities in model training and analytics, but engineers should look at where tokenization is used and, if possible, hash data at ingestion time
Never hash or tokenize data
Tokenization is only for images
Hashing is always unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book recommends tokenization for anonymization and hashing at ingestion time where possible.

questions.question: What is a "broken-glass process," and when is it used?
options: A process for bugs not reproducible without live data: require at least two people to approve access to sensitive data in production, with access tightly scoped to a particular issue and an expiration date
A process for granting permanent production access
A process for deleting production data
A process for testing without any data
questions.explanation: The book describes the broken-glass process for limited, approved, expiring production sensitive-data access.

questions.question: What does the book warn about "naive technological solutions to human problems" like encryption?
options: Encryption and tokenization are often treated like privacy magic bullets, but most cloud storage and databases already encrypt at rest and in motion — the real problems are usually access problems, and one must still tightly manage access to the encryption key, so watch out for ritualistic encryption
Encryption always solves privacy problems
Access control is never the issue
Extra encryption layers are always necessary
questions.explanation: The book says data access problems are more common than encryption problems and warns against ritualistic encryption.

questions.question: Why does the book warn about thoughtlessly hashing data without salting?
options: If someone had a customer's email, they could easily hash it and find the customer in your data — hashing without salting and other strategies may not protect privacy as well as you think
Hashing always protects privacy perfectly
Salting is never needed
Hash functions are unbreakable
questions.explanation: The book says unsalted hashes of known values like emails are trivially reversible.

questions.question: Why is monitoring critical at the ingestion stage, and what should you track?
options: If there's one stage where monitoring is critical it's ingestion, since weak monitoring means pipelines may or may not be working; track the various aspects of time (event creation, ingestion, process, processing times) and monitor uptime, latency, and data volumes processed
Monitoring is only critical at serving
Only success counts should be tracked
Time tracking is unnecessary
questions.explanation: The book emphasizes ingestion monitoring and tracking event/ingestion/process/processing times, uptime, latency, and volumes.

questions.question: What should engineers know about upstream system behavior for monitoring?
options: Be aware of the number of events generated per time interval (events/minute, events/second) and the average size of each event; the pipeline should handle both the frequency and size of ingested events
Only the total data size matters
Event frequency and size are irrelevant
Upstream behavior cannot be measured
questions.explanation: The book says to know events per interval and average event size.

questions.question: What does the book say about third-party services and incident response?
options: What you gained in lean operational efficiencies is replaced by systems outside your control; know how you'll be alerted if a third party has an outage, have a response plan, and set up failover to other servers in another zone or region if possible
Third parties never fail
No response plan is ever needed
Failover is not possible with third parties
questions.explanation: The book describes alerting, response plans, and failover for third-party dependencies.

questions.question: What does the book say about internally built ingestion processes and deployment automation?
options: Have proper testing and deployment automation to ensure code functions in production, and if the code is buggy or fails, be able to roll it back to a working version
Deployment automation is unnecessary
Rollbacks are impossible
Testing in production is recommended
questions.explanation: The book recommends testing, deployment automation, and rollback capability.

questions.question: What does the book mean by calling data a "silent killer"?
options: If quality, valid data is the foundation of success, using bad data to make decisions is much worse than having no data — bad data has caused untold damage to businesses, with data disasters sometimes called datastrophes
Data never causes problems
Bad data is always better than no data
Data quality is irrelevant
questions.explanation: The book says bad data is worse than no data and calls disasters datastrophes.
